newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Moody's confirms U.S. debt rating at Aaa.
newsitem.headline: Moody's confirms U.S. debt rating at Aaa.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service Inc said on Thursday that it confirmed the rating on the debt of the United States of America at Aaa.

"In a report issued today, Moody's Investors Service finds the credit rating of the debt of the United States of America is still solidly Aaa, despite some credit concerns," Moody's said in a statement issued from New York.
The concerns are related primarily to the nation's hefty upcoming medical and pension costs associated with an aging population, Moody's said.

But the rating agency said the concerns are far outweighed by the "size and depth of the U.S. economy, underlying political consensus, and the dominant role that the country plays in the world's major economic and political forums."

In its first in-depth credit report on the United States, Moody's adds that "when combined with comparatively low debt levels and with an intermediate-term outlook for relatively strong economic growth and low inflation, these strengths indicate very low risk of a default on U.S. Treasury bonds."
Moody's said it produced the report in response to increased investor demand for in-depth analysis on G-5 nations.

"Although Moody's has maintained a triple-A rating on debt of the United States since World War One, investor demand for in-depth analysis on the U.S. is a new phenomenon," said Christopher Mahoney, managing director of Moody's banking and sovereign ratings group.

That demand is being driven mainly by the increasing concerns of bond investors outside the U.S. over the potential credit risks stemming from the U.S. budget deficit and the country's sizable current account deficits, Moody's said.

When the debt ceiling debate threatened interest payments and certain principal payments on U.S. Treasury obligations in 1996, Moody's placed its Aaa rating on some US$300 billion of U.S. Treasury bonds under review for possible downgrade.

Moody's confirmed the government's Aaa rating when the debates were concluded; and the rating agency acknowledges that the probability of another round of debate similar to that which occurred in 1995-1996 has been reduced.

"Moody's will continue to monitor the underlying debate over the size and role of the United States government to determine if meeting the full-faith-and-credit obligations of the country could once again be at risk as a result of policy disagreements between the legislative and executive branches," Moody's said.

Last week, the U.S. Senate approved a five-year balanced budget plan, worked out between the White House and Congress. It will not be completed until both chambers act upon a final version when they return in June from a 10-day recess.
The budget plan trims Medicare by US$115 billion over five years and makes changes that are expected to keep it solvent for the next decade.

Recent improvement in federal government finances provides evidence that the U.S. will be able to keep its debt burden at manageable levels over the long term, Moody's said. Last year's budget deficit came in at US$107 billion, down from US$164 billion in 1995. "The rating agency expects that the deficit will continue to improve in 1997," the statement said.
Moody's added that at 1.4 percent of gross domestic product, the United States' budget deficit is relatively small and well below that of other G5 nations.
Moody's calculates that the net burden of servicing all U.S. foreign debt only required a net outflow of 0.1 percent of total yearly output of the economy in 1996.
"We could double or even triple that figure, and we would still be forced to conclude that the United States has very low net foreign debt," the report says.
